title: Editing Templates But Launching Stale Files
prompt:
This launch workflow edits `meta_vehicle.moos`, but the running mission still uses old ports and old behavior settings. Correct the workflow conceptually:

```bash
nsplug meta_vehicle.moos targ_vehicle.moos WARP=10 VNAME=alpha
pAntler targ_vehicle.moos
# later I edit meta_vehicle.moos, then run:
pAntler targ_vehicle.moos
```

notebook.text:
The conceptual error in your workflow is that nsplug is a template expansion tool that must be re-executed every time the template (the meta_ file) is modified
1
.
In your current sequence, when you edit meta_vehicle.moos, the changes exist only in that template file. The targ_vehicle.moos file remains a static copy of the previous version of the template. Because pAntler reads configuration parameters directly from the file passed as its argument, it continues to launch the mission using the old settings stored in the outdated targ_ file
2
3
.
Corrected Conceptual Workflow
To ensure your edits are applied, you must regenerate the target file before launching:
# 1. Generate the target file from the template
nsplug meta_vehicle.moos targ_vehicle.moos WARP=10 VNAME=alpha

# 2. Launch the mission using the newly generated target file
pAntler targ_vehicle.moos

# --- Later, after editing meta_vehicle.moos ---

# 3. RE-RUN nsplug to expand the new edits into the target file
nsplug meta_vehicle.moos targ_vehicle.moos WARP=10 VNAME=alpha

# 4. Launch again
pAntler targ_vehicle.moos

Key Rules to Remember
Never edit targ_ files directly: These files are auto-generated. Any manual changes made to a targ_ file will be overwritten and lost the next time nsplug is invoked
4
.
Automate with Launch Scripts: To avoid this manual error, most MOOS-IvP missions use a launch.sh script that handles the nsplug calls and pAntler execution in a single command
5
6
.
Clean Before Launch: It is a recommended practice to run a clean.sh script (or a "kill and clean" alias) before re-launching to ensure no dangling MOOS processes or old target files interfere with the new mission
7
8
.

This launch workflow edits meta_vehicle.moos, but the running mission still uses old ports and old behavior settings. Correct the workflow conceptually:


bash
nsplug meta_vehicle.moos targ_vehicle.moos WARP=10 VNAME=alpha
pAntler targ_vehicle.moos
# later I edit meta_vehicle.moos, then run:
pAntler targ_vehicle.moos
Thought for 14s

The mistake is that you edited the template but relaunched the already-generated target file. pAntler does not read meta_vehicle.moos; it reads targ_vehicle.moos. So unless you rerun nsplug, the mission still uses the old expanded configuration.

Correct conceptual workflow:

Bash
# 1. Edit the template
vim meta_vehicle.moos

# 2. Regenerate the concrete mission file
nsplug meta_vehicle.moos targ_vehicle.moos WARP=10 VNAME=alpha

# 3. Inspect the generated file if something seems stale
grep -n "ServerPort\|VNAME\|Behavior\|bhv" targ_vehicle.moos

# 4. Launch the generated file
pAntler targ_vehicle.moos

The key mental model:

meta_vehicle.moos  --nsplug + args-->  targ_vehicle.moos  --pAntler--> running mission

So after editing meta_vehicle.moos, this is wrong:

Bash
pAntler targ_vehicle.moos

because targ_vehicle.moos has not changed.

This is right:

Bash
nsplug meta_vehicle.moos targ_vehicle.moos WARP=10 VNAME=alpha
pAntler targ_vehicle.moos

Also watch for behavior files. If the .moos file contains something like:

behavior = targ_alpha.bhv

or launches pHelmIvP with a .bhv file, then behavior settings may come from a separate generated behavior file, not from targ_vehicle.moos itself. In that case you may need a second nsplug step:

Bash
nsplug meta_vehicle.moos targ_vehicle.moos WARP=10 VNAME=alpha
nsplug meta_vehicle.bhv  targ_vehicle.bhv  VNAME=alpha
pAntler targ_vehicle.moos

The practical debugging habit is: never trust the meta file during runtime. Inspect the generated targ_*.moos and targ_*.bhv files, because those are what the mission is actually using.

Common stale-config symptoms:

Symptom	Likely cause
Old port still used	targ_vehicle.moos was not regenerated
Old vehicle name appears	nsplug was rerun with old VNAME, or not rerun
Old behavior settings still active	.bhv file was not regenerated
Edits seem ignored	You edited meta_* but launched existing targ_*
Correct generated file, wrong runtime	You launched a different targ_*.moos than the one you inspected

A good launch script should usually regenerate targets every time:

Bash
#!/bin/bash

VNAME=alpha
WARP=10

nsplug meta_vehicle.moos targ_${VNAME}.moos WARP=$WARP VNAME=$VNAME
nsplug meta_vehicle.bhv  targ_${VNAME}.bhv  VNAME=$VNAME

pAntler targ_${VNAME}.moos

Then if the mission behaves strangely, check the generated target files first, not the templates.

Claude responded: The bug is that you're re-running pAntler on the stale targvehicle.

The bug is that you're re-running pAntler on the stale targ_vehicle.moos — the file you actually edited (meta_vehicle.moos) was never re-plugged into a new target file. Here's what's happening and how to fix it:

What's wrong
meta_vehicle.moos  ──(nsplug)──►  targ_vehicle.moos  ──(pAntler)──►  running mission
       ▲
  you edit this
                                        ▲
                         but you re-launch THIS (stale)

nsplug does a one-time substitution — it reads meta_vehicle.moos, replaces variables like WARP and VNAME, and writes the result into targ_vehicle.moos. After that, targ_vehicle.moos is a static, independent file. Editing the meta file has no effect on it until you re-run nsplug.

Corrected workflow
bash
# Step 1: plug variables into a fresh target file
nsplug meta_vehicle.moos targ_vehicle.moos WARP=10 VNAME=alpha

# Step 2: launch from the freshly generated target
pAntler targ_vehicle.moos

# --- later, after editing meta_vehicle.moos ---

# Step 3: re-plug first (regenerate targ_vehicle.moos)
nsplug meta_vehicle.moos targ_vehicle.moos WARP=10 VNAME=alpha

# Step 4: then re-launch
pAntler targ_vehicle.moos

nsplug must always precede pAntler if the meta file has changed.

Better practice: wrap it in a launch script

In real MOOS-IvP missions this is typically handled by a launch.sh that always runs both steps together, so you can never accidentally skip the plug:

bash
#!/bin/bash
# launch.sh
nsplug meta_vehicle.moos targ_vehicle.moos WARP=${WARP:-1} VNAME=${VNAME:-alpha}
pAntler targ_vehicle.moos

Then your workflow is just:

bash
# edit meta_vehicle.moos ...
./launch.sh        # nsplug + pAntler, always in sync

This way targ_vehicle.moos is always regenerated from source before launch — there's no stale intermediate file to trip over.

gemini.text:
The issue here is a classic caching/generation disconnect.

nsplug is a template processor. It takes your template file (meta_vehicle.moos), injects the variables you provide (WARP=10, VNAME=alpha), and generates a completely new, static target file (targ_vehicle.moos).

When you edit meta_vehicle.moos and immediately rerun pAntler targ_vehicle.moos, pAntler is simply reloading the old targ_vehicle.moos that was generated before your edits. It has no idea the template changed.

The Correct Workflow

You must rerun nsplug every single time you modify the template file so that your changes are compiled down into the target file before pAntler launches the MOOS community.

Bash
# 1. Generate the initial target file from the template
nsplug meta_vehicle.moos targ_vehicle.moos WARP=10 VNAME=alpha

# 2. Launch the MOOS community
pAntler targ_vehicle.moos

# --- [Later, you edit meta_vehicle.moos] ---

# 3. CRITICAL STEP: Regenerate the target file to apply your edits
nsplug meta_vehicle.moos targ_vehicle.moos WARP=10 VNAME=alpha

# 4. Launch the updated MOOS community
pAntler targ_vehicle.moos

Pro-Tip: Use a Launch Script

To avoid typing this out and forgetting the nsplug step, MOOS developers typically wrap this workflow into a short shell script (often named launch.sh):

Bash
#!/bin/bash

# Define variables
WARP=10
VNAME="alpha"

# Always generate fresh target files right before launching
nsplug meta_vehicle.moos targ_vehicle.moos WARP=$WARP VNAME=$VNAME

# Launch
pAntler targ_vehicle.moos


With a script, whenever you change meta_vehicle.moos, you just run ./launch.sh and it guarantees your newest behavior settings are baked in.
